entries.summary: Today, we’re launching the Kotlin Security Newsletter, a single place where you can track security fixes across Kotlin and its ecosystem.
entries.text: Today, we’re launching the Kotlin Security Newsletter, a single place where you can track security fixes across Kotlin and its ecosystem. We’ll collect recent security fixes across the projects we cover in one digest, publish it on our blog, and send it to your inbox, so you don’t have to follow each Kotlin library or tool update separately. We will also include broader ecosystem security news if it affects Kotlin applications. The newsletter covers topics relevant to Android, server-side, and Kotlin Multiplatform development. We aim to publish about once a month, when there’s something to share. Subscribe to the Kotlin Security Newsletter Why it matters now You probably noticed more security updates than usual this year. One of the latest examples is the quarterly OpenJDK update published in October 2026. It lists 54 fixed vulnerabilities, which is three times as many as any previous update since OpenJDK started publishing them in 2019. These days, security research is moving faster across the industry, and AI tools help researchers find issues in widely used code. Finding and fixing more issues is a good thing, but it also means more updates for your team to track, assess, and apply. The Kotlin team sees exactly the same trend. So far this year, we’ve published 10 security fixes for Kotlin, Ktor, Exposed, and the kotlinx libraries, compared with one in each of the previous two years. entries.summary: December is almost here, and so is one of our favorite coding traditions!
entries.text: December is almost here, and so is one of our favorite coding traditions! We’re excited to take part in Advent of Code once again and invite you to join us for another season of festive puzzles, clever Kotlin solutions, and friendly competition. Advent of Code is a great opportunity to learn something new and have fun along the way. A welcoming community in Kotlinlang Slack, where you can exchange ideas, share solutions, and help each other out. Kotlin leaderboards and exclusive prizes for the top performer, a randomly selected participant, and an outstanding community contributor Four days of festive coding, live From December 1 to 4, join Sebastian and a different guest each day as they work through the Advent of Code puzzles in Kotlin. entries.summary: In July, we released the Kotlin Benchmark – a collection of 105 real repository-level tasks for evaluating AI coding agents’ work with Kotlin.
entries.text: In July, we released the Kotlin Benchmark – a collection of 105 real repository-level tasks for evaluating AI coding agents’ work with Kotlin. Since then, we’ve updated it to be more representative of what Kotlin teams do, with more reliable results and more data to help you choose an agent-model configuration. The new tasks require changes across multiple files, come from projects in different Kotlin domains, and include code from private repositories. To prevent reward hacking and improve the reliability of our results, we restricted network access when agents solve open-source tasks, so they can’t look up a fix that has already been published. We also set 30-minute-per-task resolution time limit for each configuration, balancing the additional time required to solve complex problems with the need for a manageable evaluation time. See the latest Kotlin Benchmark results What’s new Harder tasks: The collection of tasks now focuses on medium- and high-complexity problems that require multi-step reasoning, debugging, and changes across multiple files. Simple single-file edits have been filtered out. Open-source and closed-source tasks: Of the 100 tasks, 70 come from open-source GitHub repositories and 30 from private JetBrains ones, where neither the code nor the fix is available online. entries.title: Kotlin Benchmark 2.0: How AI Coding Agents Handle Harder Tasks and Closed-Source Code

entries.summary: The Kotlin Toolchain helps you build and ship multiplatform apps faster, with less setup and configuration.
entries.text: The Kotlin Toolchain helps you build and ship multiplatform apps faster, with less setup and configuration. Its CLI provides a unified workflow for building, running, testing, and publishing apps for Android, iOS, desktop, and web, whether you’re developing with AI agents or writing code yourself. Kotlin Toolchain 0.14 makes it easier to publish iOS apps to TestFlight and brings improvements to agentic development workflows, along with several other enhancements. Install Kotlin Toolchain Or try this prompt in your favorite agent: Create a new Kotlin Multiplatform app for Android, iOS, desktop, and web with the Kotlin Toolchain CLI (https://kotlin-toolchain.org/latest). Copy To access the latest Kotlin Toolchain features from your IDE, use IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.4 (or newer) or Android Studio Rabbit 1 | 2026.2.1 (or newer). Make sure the latest version of the Kotlin Toolchain plugin is installed. iOS application publishing You can now publish iOS apps using the kotlin publish testflight command. This launches an easy publishing flow that guides you through most of the setup and steps required to publish a new application to TestFlight for the first time. After the first publication, you can publish updates automatically using the same command. The command will ask for an App Store Connect access token (Apple Developer Program membership is required, as usual), which is a standard way to authorize automations to publish applications in App Store Connect. entries.summary: The Kotlin Multiplatform Contest is back! Students and recent graduates, turn your idea into a cross-platform project with Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP).
entries.text: The Kotlin Multiplatform Contest is back! Students and recent graduates, turn your idea into a cross-platform project with Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP). The authors of the top three projects will each win a trip to KotlinConf 2027 in Kraków, Poland, with conference tickets, travel, and accommodation covered by the Kotlin Foundation. Authors of all other valid entries will receive Kotlin souvenirs. Submissions are open until December 7, 2026. Join the contest Your project can be a game, a developer utility, a productivity app, an experiment with AI, or something entirely different. It needs to be created specifically for the contest, use KMP, and run on at least two platforms. Target Android, iOS, desktop, web, backend, or beyond. Last year, we received 88 submissions, with 76 eligible entries from more than 30 countries. Participants built everything from AI-powered learning tools to social-impact projects and accessibility apps. We can’t wait to see what you build this year! entries.summary: Google Summer of Code 2026 has wrapped up! This was the Kotlin Foundation’s fourth year participating in GSoC, bringing new contributors into the Kotlin open-source ecosystem through hands-on projects and mentorship.
entries.text: Google Summer of Code 2026 has wrapped up! This was the Kotlin Foundation’s fourth year participating in GSoC, bringing new contributors into the Kotlin open-source ecosystem through hands-on projects and mentorship. This year, two projects successfully reached completion, tackling two areas of the ecosystem: improving recursion support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend and building a global picture of where Kotlin is taught. Congratulations to Ayako Hayasaka and Mark Seif Khalil, and a huge thank-you to our mentors for supporting them throughout the program! Here’s more on what they accomplished. Tail call support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend Contributor: Ayako Hayasaka Mentor: Charlie Zhang (JetBrains) Ayako’s project added support for WebAssembly tail-call instructions to the Kotlin/Wasm backend. The compiler can now detect calls in tail position and emit return_call or return_call_ref, helping recursive Kotlin/Wasm programs avoid increasing the call stack. In Ayako’s benchmarks, several recursive patterns became 1.7–4.3x faster at a recursion depth of 10,000. At a depth of one million, the same programs crashed without tail calls and completed successfully with them. Testing the change on real-world projects also revealed an unexpected performance regression in V8. entries.title: Google Summer of Code 2026 With the Kotlin Foundation: Recap

entries.summary: The KotlinConf 2027 Call for Papers is now open! We invite developers from across the Kotlin community to bring their ideas, experiences, and expertise to the stage in Kraków.
entries.text: The KotlinConf 2027 Call for Papers is now open! We invite developers from across the Kotlin community to bring their ideas, experiences, and expertise to the stage in Kraków. Do you have a Kotlin lesson or discovery that could help other developers? Perhaps you solved a difficult technical problem, introduced Kotlin into an existing codebase, built something unexpected, or learned valuable lessons from an approach that did not go according to plan. That experience could become a KotlinConf talk. Submit your proposal However, turning an idea into a convincing conference proposal can be challenging, especially if you’ve never submitted one before. How do you know whether your experience is worth sharing? What do reviewers notice first? How detailed should your abstract be? And how can you make a familiar topic stand out? To help you prepare your submission, we asked Kotlin developers, developer advocates, experienced speakers, and KotlinConf program committee members what makes a strong proposal. Alongside practical advice for shaping your title, abstract, and takeaways, we have added a new section answering an especially important question: What do reviewers notice first when they open a proposal? First-time speaker? Submit your idea anyway! It’s easy to assume that a KotlinConf talk must begin with a groundbreaking discovery, a major production system, or years of speaking experience. entries.text: This article was written by an external contributor. Aniket Bhattacharyea Aniket is a Mathematics postgraduate who has a passion for computers and software. He likes to explore various areas related to coding and works as a web developer using Ruby on Rails and Next.JS. Website Yuri Geronimus’s four-year-old son once asked him what his job was. Yuri told him he writes books: books that describe what he wants to change in the physical world. His son didn’t fully get it. Neither would most engineers: if you understand the words in your application code, you build good systems. If you don’t, you build bugs. That’s the spine of Yuri Geronimus’s KotlinConf 2026 talk, “Kotlin as a Safety Net: Type-Driven Reliability in the Finance Industry”. Yuri is an architect at Verifone, where he works across payment terminals, gateways, and the systems that connect them to banks and regulators in the EMEA region. His method, in one line: write code in the exact words of the regulator or card network specs, and let the compiler enforce it. Enforce not by discipline, but by the compiler. entries.summary: The Kotlin Toolchain is a unified entry point into Kotlin. It lets you build JVM, Android, iOS, multiplatform, and server-side applications with a simple declarative configuration.
entries.text: The Kotlin Toolchain is a unified entry point into Kotlin. It lets you build JVM, Android, iOS, multiplatform, and server-side applications with a simple declarative configuration. With the release of v0.13, we now recommend the Kotlin Toolchain for most new Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) projects. Earlier this year, we promoted the Kotlin Toolchain to Alpha. Since then, our Slack channels and issue tracker have been very active. So many of you in the community have joined us to create a great build experience for Kotlin. Thank you – your continuous feedback helped us get here! Not using the Kotlin Toolchain yet? Experience automated environment setup and an intuitive CLI that works well with your AI agents. Install Kotlin Toolchain To access the latest Kotlin Toolchain features from your IDE, use IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3, Android Studio Rabbit 1 | 2026.2.1 (or newer). Make sure the latest version of the Kotlin Toolchain plugin is installed. How the Kotlin Toolchain simplifies getting started Getting started with Kotlin Multiplatform often means working with unfamiliar platforms. Android developers might be discovering iOS for the first time, while other teams are expanding to web or desktop. Every platform comes with its own tools to install and build configurations to understand. The Kotlin Toolchain changes that. entries.summary: Starting with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 and Android Studio Rabbit 2 | 2026.2.2, we’re discontinuing Swift language IDE features in the Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) plugin.
entries.text: Starting with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 and Android Studio Rabbit 2 | 2026.2.2, we’re discontinuing Swift language IDE features in the Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) plugin. This includes editing, syntax highlighting, and navigation within Swift files and between Swift and Kotlin. Running iOS applications and debugging Kotlin code on iOS will remain fully supported. Kotlin/Native functionality, such as Swift Export and importing Swift packages into Kotlin projects, is not affected. The existing Swift functionality will remain available in earlier versions of IntelliJ IDEA, Android Studio, and the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin, though these older versions will not receive further updates. Background We originally developed Swift support for AppCode (our since-discontinued iOS IDE) and for working directly with Xcode projects. This technology was later adapted for Fleet’s polyglot capabilities and, most recently, for working with mixed Kotlin–Swift codebases using the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin. While analyzing feature adoption, we found that active usage was limited and steadily declining. Our telemetry and user research showed that most iOS developers working on KMP projects prefer using Xcode for Swift development, while teams that primarily work in the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin increasingly use Kotlin and Compose Multiplatform.
